detail.abstract:
Jones (1995) models long-run growth as a population-bounded process 
in which research output scales with the human research workforce. 
This paper argues that artificial intelligence renders that aggregation 
insufficient, because AI systems can scale the digitally executable 
partition of research tasks without scaling the physically constrained 
partition. The central formal result (Theorem 1) is that the 
amplification of effective research labor in sector s is bounded by 
μ_s = min(Φ(K,M), d_s/(1-d_s)), where Φ is AI capacity and d_s is 
the sector's digitally executable task share. Embedding this into the 
Jones idea production function, Theorem 2 establishes a steady-state 
bifurcation: sectors with validation-stage digital task share below a 
time-varying threshold obey the Jones semi-endogenous growth rate 
exactly; sectors above it grow at the strictly higher capital-driven 
rate. Corollary 2.1 establishes that Regime II is transient for all 
sectors with finite d_s^V: as AI capital grows, sectors return to the 
Jones attractor. Only the formalized mathematics subfield — where 
d_s^V = 1 by Lemma 1 — permanently escapes the Jones ceiling. 
Proposition 2 formalizes the measurement implication: the Bloom et al. 
(2020) research productivity measure generates systematic downward bias 
as AI capital grows in Regime I sectors. The pharmaceutical evidence — 
elevated Phase I success rates alongside unchanged Phase II rates — is 
consistent with Regime I dynamics. The mathematics evidence — IMO 
gold-medal performance, miniF2F near-saturation, FrontierMath 2% to 
40% in 14 months — establishes the empirical pole of permanent 
Regime II. Replication data available at: 
https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/FA75PH

detail.abstract: The article starts with an introduction to the “economics” of Initial Public Offerings (IPOs), the “economics” of book-building and clarification of the important role played by institutional investors in determining the final offer price and the allocation of shares. The article then goes on to analyse the interrelation between the provisions of the CDR 2017/565 supplementing MiFID II (in particular Articles 38-40) and the complex system established by the PR (in particular under Article 17) and the MAR (especially with respect to market manipulation) during IPOs for the purposes of investor protection from a European perspective. The question addressed is the extent to which the IPO conflict of interest rules laid down by the CDR 2017/565, particularly where they may give rise to market abuse, can function as an ex ante preventive mechanism, as opposed to relying on ex post sanctions for market manipulation. The article then considers the Italian IPO system by analysing certain practices that may be considered to be problematic in the light of the CDR 2017/565 rules. In particular, the article argues that, even if the important role played by institutional investors in final price determination is accepted, in “problematic” IPOs the practice of shifting shares to retail investors (with clawback clauses) may be suspected as amounting to market abuse in terms of market manipulation also based on the CDR 2017/565 rules. As a further step, it should be possible to empirically analyse the extent to which the post-2018 regulatory regime has implied a reduction in the use of clawback clauses, thereby mitigating the risk of enforcement for market abuse.

title: Educational-Political Game: Institutional Choice of Class Solidification and Cognitive Evolution

detail.title: Educational-Political Game: Institutional Choice of Class Solidification and Cognitive Evolution
detail.abstract: Traditional educational theories have long regarded education as a neutral institution for knowledge transmission, talent cultivation, and social selection, yet they generally avoid its underlying political logic, class function, and evolutionary essence. Based on the author's original Genetic Five-Level Evolution Theory and the Positive-Negative Extreme Environment Evolution Theory, this paper constructs a complete theoretical framework covering biological foundation, environmental mechanism, political choice, and social outcome to deconstruct and deduce the modern education system at a fundamental level. This study demonstrates that an educational model is not a technical design, but the result of a political game between governance costs and social evolution. Negative-extreme education, characterized by pressure, punishment, competition, and fear, locks individuals in low-level genetic states by generating survival anxiety to realize selective evolution that eliminates the majority and screens only a tiny minority, ultimately serving class solidification and social stability. Positive-extreme education, characterized by security, satisfaction, rational guidance, and independent development, activates cognitive potential through low-anxiety environment to achieve inclusive evolution that improves the majority and optimizes the whole, thus promoting large-scale class mobility and social restructuring. Through logical deduction, mechanism verification, counterevidence elimination, and realistic comparison, this paper completes theoretical testing and proves that the nature of education is an environmental regulatory tool of genetic cognition, and institutional choice determines evolutionary direction. This paper subverts the presupposition of traditional pedagogy and provides an original, rigorous, deducible, and verifiable fundamental scientific framework for educational essence, institutional reform, social equity, and political-economic analysis.

title: A Study on Passenger Satisfaction and Service Quality in Indian Airlines

detail.title: A Study on Passenger Satisfaction and Service Quality in Indian Airlines
detail.abstract: Passenger satisfaction has become an important factor in the success of airlines, especially in today's competitive aviation industry. With the growth of air travel in India, passengers now expect better service quality, timely operations, and a comfortable travel experience. This study focuses on understanding the level of passenger satisfaction and evaluating the quality of services provided by Indian airlines. The research is based on primary data collected through a survey of airline passengers. Various factors such as punctuality, staff behaviour, in-flight services, and ticket pricing have been considered. The results show that service quality plays a major role in influencing passenger satisfaction. The study also highlights areas where airlines need improvement to enhance overall customer experience and maintain competitiveness in the market.

title: Global Cooperative Alignment Framework for Sovereign States in Pursuit of Stable Peace and Freedom:  Moving Towards Global Peace Establishment

detail.title: Global Cooperative Alignment Framework for Sovereign States in Pursuit of Stable Peace and Freedom:  Moving Towards Global Peace Establishment
detail.abstract:
This Green Paper proposes a Global Cooperative Alignment Framework (GCAF) designed to address structural limitations in existing international governance systems. Despite the presence of global institutions aimed at maintaining peace and stability, interstate conflict persists due to the absence of a unified, equilibrium-based coordination structure among sovereign states.
The proposed framework introduces a minimal set of civilizational constraints, a stability-based evaluation model, and a structured intellectual resolution system to transform interstate conflict dynamics. The objective is to shift global interactions from conflict-prone behavior toward a stable cooperative equilibrium where peace, freedom, and civilizational development emerge as self-sustaining outcomes.

title: Beyond Disinformation: Future Imaginaries as Cognitive Stability Architectures

detail.title: Beyond Disinformation: Future Imaginaries as Cognitive Stability Architectures

detail.abstract:
Contemporary research on disinformation and influence has increasingly shifted from content-centric to state-based models of cognition. These models demonstrate that belief formation and rigidity depend strongly on affective and executive conditions rather than on informational accuracy alone.

However, existing frameworks remain incomplete. While they identify mechanisms of destabilization and outline structural countermeasures, they do not sufficiently address the cultural layer through which cognitive stability is socially reproduced and maintained.

This paper introduces future imaginaries as a class of cultural structures that function as cognitive stability architectures. Unlike ideological systems, which stabilize cognition through normative closure and identity binding, future imaginaries provide orientation, coherence, and anticipatory structure without suppressing epistemic flexibility.

The availability, or absence, of such imaginaries plays a critical role in determining whether societies under stress shift toward ideological rigidity or maintain adaptive cognitive openness. Rather than treating narratives as secondary cultural artifacts, this framework positions them as functional components of large-scale cognitive regulation rather than secondary cultural artifacts.

detail.title: Synergizing Leadership and Well-Being: A Qualitative Study of Adaptive Mechanisms for Sustainable Growth

detail.abstract:
Abstract 

Technology-intensive enterprises increasingly operate under conditions of high velocity, distributed interdependence, and persistent uncertainty, where leadership influence is realized less through formal authority than through organizational mechanisms that translate intent into coherent action. Despite substantial investment in leadership development, many organizations continue to experience chronic misalignment manifested as priority volatility, decision churn, and role ambiguity alongside rising concerns about employee well-being and long-term sustainability. Addressing this gap, this interpretivist qualitative study examines how leadership practices are enacted as alignment mechanisms across hierarchical levels, and how employee well-being mediates the relationship between leadership–alignment dynamics and sustainable organizational growth.

Using purposive, role-stratified sampling, semi-structured interviews were conducted with professionals across three organizational strata within a technology-intensive enterprise. Data were analyzed through rigorous thematic analysis with iterative coding, cross-case comparison, reflexive memorandum, and an explicit audit trail. Six themes emerged: leadership as interpretive framing and meaning stabilization, alignment as enacted infrastructure (decision rights, cadence, boundaries), uncertainty-driven cognitive load as the primary well-being stressor; psychological safety erosion under blame and unpredictability, well-being as organizational renewal capacity, and instinctive leadership as conditionally adaptive, producing short-term coherence but requiring explainability and learning conversion to sustain trust.

The findings advance an integrated Leadership-Alignment-Well-Being-Sustainability (LAWS) pathway, demonstrating that sustainable growth in technology-intensive contexts depends on leadership’s capacity to institutionalize alignment mechanisms and protect human sustainability under volatility.

detail.abstract: High-field infrastructures do not fail at the operational level; they fail at the structural threshold where continuity becomes unsustainable. This paper introduces Structural Continuity Load (SCL) as the pre-rupture limit that determines whether a system can maintain coherence under increasing field tension. SCL is not a metric, but a structural condition: the point were stability transitions from resilience to fragility. Conventional systems,ports, logistics, defence, governance, capital, cannot detect this threshold because they operate within the operational layer, while SCL exists exclusively in the structural layer. UNC sYstEm L provides the mechanism required to identify, stabilize, and transform this threshold before rupture becomes visible.

title: THE FORMATION LAYER AND LEADERSHIP FAILURE

detail.title: THE FORMATION LAYER AND LEADERSHIP FAILURE
detail.abstract: The global investment in leadership development has reached historically elevated levels. The outcomes have not. Leadership failure rates-defined as derailment, underperformance, or inability to sustain behavioral change under pressure-have remained structurally stable despite sustained investment in training, coaching, and organizational development programs. This paper argues that this failure is not a delivery problem. It is a diagnostic problem. The existing leadership development category intervenes at the behavioral symptom layer-the observable expressions of leadership breakdown. It does not reach, and was not designed to reach, the formation layer: the developmental substrate constructed in childhood that determines whether a leader can access judgment, hold authority, regulate affect, and sustain integrity when it costs something to do so. This paper establishes nine universal leadership failure modes-the breakdown patterns documented across five independent derailment research traditions-and maps each one to its precise developmental origin in the formation layer. For each failure mode, it names the existing frameworks that address it, locates the structural ceiling of each, and proposes the specific formation-layer intervention target, entry point, and measurable output that the existing category cannot produce. The paper concludes with four research questions constituting the empirical validation agenda for this class of intervention. This paper cites the Behavioral Operating System category definition (El Shazly & Adly, 2026) as the broader architecture within which the formation layer concept is situated, and stands as an independent contribution to that research agenda.

title: Signal-Pattern Analysis (SPA): A Method for Analysing Strategic Behaviour in International Relations

detail.title: Signal-Pattern Analysis (SPA): A Method for Analysing Strategic Behaviour in International Relations
detail.abstract:
This article introduces and formalises signal-pattern analysis (SPA) as a methodological framework for analysing strategic behaviour in international relations. Contemporary international processes are increasingly characterised by complexity, strategic ambiguity, and the proliferation of signalling behaviour, while existing theoretical approaches remain limited in their ability to capture dynamic patterns of interaction in real time.

SPA addresses this gap by conceptualising international processes as systems of signals that generate recurring behavioural patterns. The framework is based on the identification and functional classification of signals, their aggregation into patterns, and their interpretation within a dual-layer analytical structure combining functional and interpretive levels.

The article develops the core components of SPA, including the definition of signals, a typology of functional roles, a mechanism of pattern formation, and a structured analytical process linking signals to strategic behaviour. It demonstrates how SPA enables the reconstruction of strategic logic by connecting micro-level observations with macro-level patterns.

The analytical utility of the framework is illustrated through selected cases of U.S. interaction with Russia and Iran, showing how recurring signal configurations reflect broader strategic approaches. The findings suggest that SPA provides a systematic and flexible tool for analysing complex environments of strategic interaction, particularly under conditions of uncertainty, hybrid conflict, and multi-level competition.

The article contributes to methodological development in international relations by offering a framework capable of capturing dynamic strategic behaviour beyond post hoc interpretation, and by bridging the gap between empirical observation and theoretical explanation.

The SPA framework is presented in full in:
Tymoshenko, N. (2026). Signal-Pattern Analysis (SPA): A Method for Analysing Strategic Behaviour in International Relations.

title: Game Theory as a Confined Experiment The Prisoner's Dilemma, the Rule-Setting Police, and the False Rationality of Caged Players

detail.title: Game Theory as a Confined Experiment The Prisoner's Dilemma, the Rule-Setting Police, and the False Rationality of Caged Players
detail.abstract: Classical game theory presents the prisoner's dilemma as a fundamental insight into strategic interaction. Two suspects, A and B, are interrogated separately. Each can cooperate with the other by remaining silent or defect by betraying the other. The payoffs are structured so that defection is the dominant strategy for both, leading to mutual defection even though mutual cooperation would make both better off. This paper argues that the prisoner's dilemma, as classically formulated, is not a neutral analysis of rational choice but a biased narrative that conceals the role of the rule-setter. In the standard story, the police officer C designs the interrogation rules, sets the payoff matrix, isolates the suspects, and then steps back to watch them choose. C is treated as part of the background, not as a player. This paper shows that C is not a neutral observer. C is the true power holder. C designs a confined space in which A and B are forced to choose between two options, both of which benefit C more than they benefit A or B. Within this cage, A and B are told that they are rational. Their rationality, however, is a false rationality. It is rationality within a fixed, narrow, externally imposed set of options. True rationality, this paper argues, is not the ability to choose optimally within given rules. True rationality is the ability to question the rules, to step outside the cage, and to redesign the game itself. Truly rational actors do not accept C's rules. They engage in opportunity-cost calculation beyond the sentence matrix, make side payments to each other, establish informal norms and loyalty contracts, use deterrence and retaliation to change the expected costs of defection, and leverage identity and hierarchy to restructure the power relations of the game. These behaviors are not irrational. They are the behaviors of players who refuse to play C's game. The paper concludes that classical game theory is not a neutral tool for understanding strategic interaction. It is an ideology that normalizes the cage. It teaches players to be clever monkeys fighting inside a zoo while the zookeeper watches. True rationality is not winning inside the cage. True rationality is walking out of the cage or becoming the one who builds it.

title: From Alliance to Network: The Türkiye-United Kingdom Strategic Partnership and the Evolution of the Security Architecture of NATO 2.0. Adem Bilgin (Association of Digital Ecosystem Governance, Ankara/ Türkiye
affiliations: Association of Digital Ecosystem Governance and Development Research

detail.title: From Alliance to Network: The Türkiye-United Kingdom Strategic Partnership and the Evolution of the Security Architecture of NATO 2.0. Adem Bilgin (Association of Digital Ecosystem Governance, Ankara/ Türkiye
detail.abstract: This article examines the transformation of alliance structures in the contemporary international system through an in-depth analysis of the 2026 Strategic Partnership Framework between Türkiye and the United Kingdom. Departing from classical alliance theory, which conceptualizes security organizations as hierarchical and relatively rigid formations, the study argues that the evolving structure of NATO reflects a gradual shift toward a networked security architecture characterized by flexibility, modularity, and multi-level coordination. The central research question asks how the Türkiye-United Kingdom strategic partnership contributes to this transformation without precipitating institutional disintegration. Methodologically, the article adopts a qualitative case study approach supported by document analysis and an actor-based geopolitical framework. It introduces an "Actor Reaction Matrix" to systematically assess how major global actors-including the United States, European Union, Russia, and China-interpret and respond to the emerging partnership. The findings suggest that the Türkiye-UK framework functions as a strategic node within a broader transition from alliance-based security to networked configurations, enabling middle powers to exercise greater agency while remaining embedded within existing institutional structures. The article further advances a theoretical contribution by integrating the concept of Relative Universalism into international security studies, demonstrating how pluralistic norm production and flexible alignment strategies can coexist with enduring alliance commitments. It concludes that NATO is not undergoing collapse but rather adaptive reconfiguration, wherein middle power alignments such as the Türkiye-United Kingdom partnership act as catalysts for systemic transformation. This evolution reflects a broader shift toward a fragmented yet interconnected multipolar order, where security is increasingly produced through overlapping networks rather than singular alliance hierarchies.

detail.title: African Historical Biography Series: Chief Micheal Soyebo Sowole of Ipara-Remo: Legislator, Diplomat, and Public Servant of Western Nigeria
detail.abstract: Chief Micheal Soyebo Sowole hails from Ipara-Remo, in present-day Ogun State, Nigeria. As a senior member of Chief Obafemi Awolowo's Action Group (AG) and a close personal friend of the Premier himself, Sowole served as a member of the Western Region House of Assembly (WRHA), moved the landmark 14 June 1955 legislative motion that gave the first parliamentary recognition to what became the Midwest Region of Nigeria in 1963, and subsequently represented the Western Region as Agent-General and Ambassador in London. He later served as a commissioner in the post-1967 Western State government. Despite his evident significance to the First Republic era (1960-1966), Sowole has received minimal sustained scholarly attention. This working paper, drawing on contemporaneous newspaper records, the Western Region House of Assembly Debates (14 June 1955), royal memoirs, archival photographic captions from Paul Popper Limited (1956) and Getty Images/Keystone (1958), and published personal interviews, presents the most comprehensive account of his career assembled to date. Three findings are offered as new contributions to the historical record: (1) that Sowole received 82 votes to Awolowo's 81 in the 1951 Remo Electoral College, a result unreported in prior scholarship; (2) the full dialogue of the 1956 ministerial withdrawal episode; and (3) the identification of 45A Kensington Gardens, London, as a significant diplomatic and social hub for Yoruba elites in Britain in the late 1950s.

title: Structural Constraints and the Generalized Theory of Games Breaking the Prisoner's Dilemma Through Opportunity Cost Asymmetry and Side Payments

detail.title: Structural Constraints and the Generalized Theory of Games Breaking the Prisoner's Dilemma Through Opportunity Cost Asymmetry and Side Payments
detail.abstract: Classical game theory holds that in a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, mutual defection is the unique Nash equilibrium. This conclusion rests on five implicit assumptions: symmetry of opportunity costs among players, the impossibility of external side payments, a one-dimensional choice space, the absence of social norms or ideological constraints, and the absence of postgame retaliation or deterrence. This paper argues that when these assumptions are relaxed, the prisoner's dilemma can be resolved in favor of mutual cooperation or a superior outcome in which one player achieves higher gains while the other also benefits. The paper introduces a generalized framework in which players face asymmetric opportunity costs and can engage in side payments backed by enforceable contracts or credible deterrence. Using the case of a highopportunity-cost player and a low-opportunity-cost player, the paper demonstrates that the high-cost player can pay the low-cost player an amount that exceeds the low-cost player's opportunity cost of defection while remaining below the high-cost player's own loss from defection. Under these conditions, both players achieve higher utility than under mutual defection. The paper extends this analysis to oligopolistic markets, where a dominant firm can use monopoly rents to buy out the production capacity of smaller firms, transforming a zero-sum price war into a positive-sum outcome for all participants. The paper further incorporates ideological constraints, hierarchical relationships, and deterrence into the utility function, showing that any factor that sufficiently increases the cost of defection makes cooperation rational even in a one-shot game. The paper concludes that the prisoner's dilemma is not an inherent property of strategic situations but a consequence of narrow assumptions about the structure of payoffs and the constraints on player behavior. When opportunity costs are asymmetric and side payments are permitted, the dilemma dissolves, and both players can achieve outcomes superior to mutual defection.

title: Early Warning Signals for Corporate Financial Collapse: A Cross-Validated Rate Mismatch Criterion Approach with AUC = 0.963

detail.title: Early Warning Signals for Corporate Financial Collapse: A Cross-Validated Rate Mismatch Criterion Approach with AUC = 0.963

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study used only publicly available financial market data. No human participants were involved. Ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding received. This research was conducted independently.

detail.abstract: Corporate financial collapse imposes severe social costs-job losses, pension destruction, and systemic contagion-yet reliable early warning systems with multi-month lead times remain elusive. Drawing on Critical Slowing Down (CSD) theory from nonlinear dynamics and the Isomorphic Systems Consolidation (ISC) framework, we apply variance-based early warning signal methods to 45 documented corporate collapse cases spanning 1990-2023, including bank failures, fraud collapses, and industrial insolvencies. Using rolling variance computed over optimised windows (60-90 days for financial ratios; 90-180 days for equity time series) with richer feature construction than prior work, the model achieves AUC = 0.963 (95% CI [0.921, 0.994]) on held-out test cases, substantially outperforming credit rating agency benchmarks (typical AUC 0.70-0.85). Mean warning time was 174 days (SD = 89), with a maximum of 305 days. The variance-based criterion significantly outperforms AR1-based and joint criteria in this domain, consistent with the mean-reversion boundary condition identified in companion work (Malone, 2026b). These results establish CSD-based early warning as a viable complement to traditional financial distress prediction, capturing instability dynamics not reflected in accounting ratios or credit spreads alone.

title: State Governance Under Uncertainty: Human Dignity and Monetary Sustainability as Goal and Precondition

detail.title: State Governance Under Uncertainty: Human Dignity and Monetary Sustainability as Goal and Precondition

detail.abstract:
This research series develops a model of state governance that remains operable under conditions of fundamental uncertainty. The central thesis: State action requires clarification of two questions. First: What is the ultimate goal? Second: What are the functional preconditions without which this goal cannot be achieved?

The series argues: The ultimate goal of the state is human dignity—not prosperity, growth, or stability. The central functional precondition is monetary sustainability. Both stand in a circular stabilization relationship: Without monetary sustainability, dignity cannot be financed. Without dignity, monetary sovereignty cannot be legitimized.

The model analyzes five core problems: (1) monetary sustainability as a trust resource, (2) human dignity as the ultimate state goal, (3) chance, emergence, and system dynamics, (4) the reproduction of moral actors, (5) navigation in international interdependence. It demonstrates that control destroys future viability. Navigation requires moral actors willing to take responsibility when rules fail. The model offers no recipes, but criteria for decisions under uncertainty.

Note: This paper series is written in German.

title: From Coercion to Design: Labor Markets, Subsistence, and the Transition Problem

detail.title: From Coercion to Design: Labor Markets, Subsistence, and the Transition Problem
detail.abstract: This paper develops a theory of labor markets based on subsistence constraints, showing that once baseline consumption is guaranteed, labor supply becomes a participation problem rather than a marginal choice. The observed equilibrium is therefore distorted, with wages below true reservation levels. Removing subsistence creates a transition problem, as participation collapses unless compensation meets the threshold. The paper proposes a state-contingent, self-extinguishing policy rule that ensures participation while preserving incentives, generating monotone and convergent dynamics in which wages and productivity rise and subsidies vanish. The main contribution is to shift the focus from equilibrium outcomes to transition path design.

title: Imputed Survey Dates and Spurious Effects of the Minimum Legal Drinking Age: A Comment on Alonso-Armesto et al. (2026)

detail.title: Imputed Survey Dates and Spurious Effects of the Minimum Legal Drinking Age: A Comment on Alonso-Armesto et al. (2026)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial conflicts of interest. The author has previously published research on the same topic and using the same data as the paper under comment (Bagues and Villa, 2025), which may constitute a non-financial competing interest. This prior work is explicitly acknowledged in the comment.

detail.abstract: Alonso-Armesto et al. (2026) estimate the impact of an increase in the minimum legal drinking age (MLDA) in three Spanish regions using a difference-in-discontinuities design. A central claim of their paper is that increasing the MLDA reduces not only alcohol consumption but also tobacco and marijuana use. We show that these findings are spurious due to a fundamental but unacknowledged limitation of the database: it does not allow precise measurement of respondents' age at survey. The authors attempt to circumvent this problem by combining information on month and year of birth with an imputed single survey date for each region-wave cell, a procedure that generates severe measurement error in the running variable. Fieldwork spans multiple months, yet the same date is assigned to all respondents, and strikingly, in nearly half the waves the imputed dates fall outside the official survey period altogether. More critically, these imputation choices introduce a confounder that is asymmetrically distributed across treatment and control cells. The authors assign January 1st-Spain's schoolyear enrollment cutoff-as the survey date in 67% of control cells (MLDA=16) but only 20% of treated ones (MLDA=18), so that their estimated discontinuity captures relative age effects rather than MLDA impact. All significant results disappear once birth-month fixed effects are included. The authors' inference is further undermined by their reliance on asymptotic approximations for cluster-robust standard errors in a context with only six clusters; under wild cluster bootstrap or heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors, significant results similarly vanish.

detail.title: Global Knowledge and the Local Emergence of Environmental Goods. The Role of Foreign Multinationals in Turkiye
detail.abstract:
This paper examines how multinational enterprises foster the emergence and diffusion of environmental
goods (EG) production in Turkiye (2005-2015). Using detailed firm-product data and product-space
relatedness measures, we show that related productive capabilities embedded in foreign affiliates significantly
increase the likelihood that a province introduces new EG, an effect stronger for EG than
for other products. At the firm level, domestic regional capabilities and firms’ own product portfolios
matter for adoption, while foreign relatedness is particularly important for more sophisticated products
and in regions lacking green knowledge and prior experience. The demand and technology channels
play a smaller, less significant role.

title: Public Narratives vs Ground Realities: The Participation Paradox in India's Growth Path (2014-2026)

detail.abstract: This study examines the divergence between high-visibility economic expansion and functional participation outcomes in India, with a focused analytical lens on Eastern regions. While recent years have witnessed significant growth in infrastructure, digital integration, and public expenditure, field-level observations and administrative evidence suggest that access to participation remains uneven across economic actors, particularly for MSMEs and locally embedded enterprises. Adopting an exploratory and pattern-oriented approach, the study integrates RTIbased administrative records, publicly available datasets, and field-level observations to identify recurring structural signals. These include concentration in market participation, constraints in enterprise scaling, fragmentation in governance systems, and a gap between formal access and effective utilization. The analysis further highlights the implications of debt-financed expansion, emphasizing the need to evaluate not only the scale of investment, but also its efficiency, outcome alignment, and distributional impact. To address these challenges, the study proposes a field-verified governance architecture based on continuous data validation, coordinated institutional functioning, and outcome-linked accountability. The findings suggest that sustainable development depends not only on economic growth, but on the credibility, accessibility, and functionality of participation pathways. Without verification-linked governance, system visibility may risk substituting for measurable outcomes rather than reliably reflecting them.

title: The Second Media Compression: How Artificial Intelligence Is Completing Structural Consolidation in American Media

detail.title: The Second Media Compression: How Artificial Intelligence Is Completing Structural Consolidation in American Media
detail.abstract: The American media industry has undergone two distinct phases of structural compression over the past four decades. The first compression is well-documented: through legislative capitulation, regulatory abdication, and sustained strategic acquisition, a fragmented ownership landscape consolidated into a small number of dominant firms. The result is an oligopoly on the output side of the media market and an oligopsony on the input side, where creative and journalistic labor is purchased, producing measurable effects on content diversity, democratic information, and labor market outcomes. This paper introduces the concept of second media compression to describe a new phase now underway. Artificial intelligence is being deployed within this already concentrated ownership structure, producing outcomes that differ fundamentally from those predicted in competitive markets. In competitive environments, AI functions as a productivity-enhancing and diversity-expanding technology. In concentrated markets, the same technology operates as a mechanism for margin capture, labor displacement, and content homogenization. The divergence is structural, not technological. The analysis traces the economic, sociopolitical, and cultural consequences of these two compressions and evaluates the limitations of existing antitrust and AI regulatory frameworks. It argues that behavioral remedies are insufficient and that structural interventions, informed by precedents such as Standard Oil and AT&T, are necessary to restore competitive conditions and preserve content diversity. The argument is informed by the author's academic training in industrial organization and direct experience in strategic planning during the AT&T divestiture.

detail.abstract: Public procurement systems play a central role in the delivery of digital transformation initiatives. However, many large-scale government technology projects continue to produce limited improvements in service outcomes despite substantial investment. This paper introduces the concept of procurement inertia-the structural tendency of procurement frameworks to prioritize procedural compliance over verified delivery outcomes. The paper identifies a critical gap in current procurement structures: the absence of independent, outcome-based verification at the point of project acceptance. While oversight mechanisms such as internal IT validation, vendor reporting, and post-hoc audits exist, these mechanisms are often fragmented, retrospective, or structurally conflicted. As a result, systems are frequently deemed "successfully implemented" without demonstrating measurable improvements in performance. This creates a condition in which accountability is diffused, delivery risk is obscured, and inefficiencies persist despite formal completion. The paper argues that without integrating independent outcome verification into procurement frameworks, digital transformation efforts will continue to replicate structural inefficiencies. It concludes by emphasizing the need for a distinct verification layer that evaluates post-deployment outcomes rather than procedural completion alone.

title: Process Inertia: The Hidden Cost of Bureaucracy

detail.title: Process Inertia: The Hidden Cost of Bureaucracy

detail.abstract: Public systems often exhibit persistent inefficiencies that are not the result of failure, but of structural stability. This paper introduces the concept of process inertia-the tendency of administrative systems to preserve existing procedures regardless of their effectiveness. Rather than self-correcting, bureaucratic processes tend to accumulate steps over time. This accumulation is driven by risk-avoidance incentives, fragmented responsibility, and the absence of continuous outcome verification. As a result, systems prioritize procedural completion over actual delivery outcomes. The paper identifies recurring structural patterns, including redundant verification rituals, repeated data entry caused by system fragmentation, endurance-based filtering of users, and the diffusion of accountability across multiple actors. These patterns collectively sustain inefficiency without triggering systemic correction. The analysis further argues that digital transformation efforts often fail to resolve these issues because they replicate existing process structures rather than redesign them. Technology accelerates execution, but does not eliminate structural friction. To address process inertia, the paper emphasizes the importance of outcome visibility. When inefficiency is measured and made observable, simplification becomes defensible, removal becomes rational, and accountability becomes actionable.

detail.abstract: This hypothesis proposes a systemic model for national rebirth based on the stabilization of the "First System" (the individual) as a prerequisite for the restoration of the "Second System" (the nation). Drawing on the Entropy Model of Uncertainty (EMU) and Big Five personality theory, we argue that prolonged sociopolitical stress has facilitated a state of "Maximum Resilience" (Rmax) in the Iranian population. This state is characterized by a voluntary shift from High Neuroticism (reactive survival) to Emotional Stability (proactive architecture). We term the historical and genetic anchor of this stability the "Cyrus Factor." This paper outlines how the optimization of individual psychological entropy creates the structural integrity necessary to re-establish a sovereign and functional national environment.

title: Theft of India (1498-1765 Ce) and Damage the Indian Economy: An Analytical Study

detail.title: Theft of India (1498-1765 Ce) and Damage the Indian Economy: An Analytical Study
detail.abstract: India's economy was a vibrant and complex mix of an advanced commercial system, thriving artisanal industries, strong inland trade routes, and lively maritime connections from the Arabian Sea to Southeast Asia. Beginning in the 1498 to 1765 AD time period, India was systematically removed from its economic prosperity due to European involvement in trading within the region. The research aims to explore how this European involvement affected the economic and political fate of India. Qualitative and Historical Research Methodologies and qualitative research are used to interpret the stages of change that took place over time within India's economic, political, and institutional structure from 1498 to 1765 due to European participation in the Indian trade market. The qualitative research approach was chosen as well in recognition of the historical context of this research. Europe established a new form of Business and Governmental partnership. The combination of the European Military Organisation and the financial resources of European nations gave rise to the potential to reconfigure the political landscape of India. In 1765, the East India Company created the first business and political structure that continues today. Conclusion-The time frame of 1498 to 1765 represented an evolution in Indian society and the institutions of that society as a result of various European Trading Companies. The Trading Companies endeavoured to monopolize the trading of goods while also dominating the political structure and military operations on the ocean, coupled with coercive collection of revenues through forced exaction, and a systematic and permanent reorganization of Indian society and institutions, enabling the Trading Companies to systematically extract immense amounts of wealth from India.

detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence technologies has precipitated an urgent imperative for coherent, effective, and globally harmonised regulatory frameworks. This paper conducts a systematic comparative analysis of three dominant paradigms: the EU AI Act (2024), the US Executive Order on Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy AI (2023), and China's Generative AI Regulations (2023). Employing a mixedmethods approach (regulatory text analysis, econometric modelling, survey data; n=1,847), we identify a "regulatory trilemma" and propose the Global AI Policy Convergence Framework (GAPCF).

title: Beating the Earnings Game: Why Do Prediction Markets Outperform Professional Analysts?
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS),  and Tsinghua University

detail.title: Beating the Earnings Game: Why Do Prediction Markets Outperform Professional Analysts?
detail.abstract: We investigate why decentralized blockchain-based prediction markets (PM) outperform traditional intermediaries in aggregating information about firm fundamentals. Using 469 firm-quarter observations from Polymarket earnings contracts, we show that PM probabilities are more accurate than analyst consensus. This advantage persists across benchmarks and is not explained by observable characteristics or trading strategies. We attribute PM superiority to four mechanisms: correction of analyst biases, continuous information updating, the wisdom of crowds, and an advantage in forecasting idiosyncratic earnings. Overall, PM aggregate timely, diverse, firm-specific signals that bypass distortions in analyst forecasts, suggesting a new layer of financial information discovery.

title: The MIET Framework: An Institutional Approach to Housing and Land Markets in the Balearic Islands

detail.title: The MIET Framework: An Institutional Approach to Housing and Land Markets in the Balearic Islands

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops the Insular Territorial Equilibrium Framework (MIET) as an institutional approach to housing and land markets in the Balearic Islands, a territory characterized by rigid land supply and strong external demand.

The central mechanism is that housing prices are determined by the marginal buyer. As external demand becomes dominant, prices are increasingly set by buyers with higher purchasing power, weakening the relationship between housing prices and local income. This leads to a structural decoupling that conventional supply-side and price-based policies fail to address.

Building on this diagnosis, the MIET proposes a functional differentiation of land into distinct segments—residential, mixed, and patrimonial—each governed by different institutional rules. This separation prevents direct competition between demand groups with heterogeneous purchasing power and restores the link between housing access and local economic conditions in the residential segment.

Rather than intervening directly on prices, the framework modifies the institutional structure under which prices are formed. The proposal is consistent with companion theoretical and empirical work on marginal-buyer dynamics and demand heterogeneity in housing markets.

The paper provides a policy-oriented framework for addressing housing affordability in small, open, and highly exposed territories.

The paper is written in Catalan. An English version is in preparation.

title: EU AI Act: Obligation-to-Control (O2C) Framework

detail.title: EU AI Act: Obligation-to-Control (O2C) Framework
detail.abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has raised a number of regulatory issues, particularly around accountability, transparency and risk management for AI systems. The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act) represents a significant attempt at creating a comprehensive regulatory framework that relies on a risk-based approach that aims to regulate the design, development and deployment of AI technologies. This paper provides a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) of the key legislative elements of the EU AI Act in order to evaluate their impact on AI Governance and Compliance. The review highlights large gaps that exist between the legislative requirements and how they translate into practice by synthesising the literature around AI regulation, explainability, accountability and risk management. The findings indicate that while the EU AI Act contains a number of useful guidelines and standards for compliance, there is no systematic mechanism for implementing these requirements into technology and organisational contexts. In particular, the concept of auditability has not been sufficiently advanced, limiting the ability to properly review and enforce compliance. In order to solve these problems, the paper introduces the Obligation-to-Control (O2C) architectural solution that uses auditability criteria and artefacts to transform regulatory obligations into control families. The compliance concept is further integrated using a reference architecture and continuous compliance methodology. This contribution addresses the challenge of linking legal theory with technical practice and therefore contributes to the growing literature on AI governance. This research will be valuable for practitioners, policymakers, and researchers who aim at building accountable AI applications within the scope of the EU AI Act.

title: MASR-DNet: A Deformable Multi-scale Spatial Context Attention Network for Aortic Valve Detection in CT and Cardiomegaly Localization in Chest X-ray Images

detail.title: MASR-DNet: A Deformable Multi-scale Spatial Context Attention Network for Aortic Valve Detection in CT and Cardiomegaly Localization in Chest X-ray Images

keywords.keywords: MASR-DNetAortic valve detectionCardiomegaly localizationDeformable convolutionMulti-scale attentionAdaptive similarity contrastive loss

detail.abstract: Accurate aortic valve detection and cardiomegaly localization in medical images are essential for diagnosis and surgical planning, yet manual identification remains time-consuming, operator-dependent, and difficult to scale. The aortic valve presents particular challenges in CT imaging due to its small size, morphological variability, and susceptibility to calcification. Cardiomegaly detection in chest X-rays is further complicated by diffuse cardiac boundaries and resolution heterogeneity across clinical sites. To address these challenges, we propose MASR-DNet, a deformable spatial-context attention network built upon a YOLO-style one-stage detection framework. The architecture integrates four specialized modules: Geometric Adaptive Deformable Convolution (GADC) for adaptive geometric modeling, Enhanced Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (EASPP) for multi-scale contextual aggregation, Multi-Scale Refinement (MSRF) for structural detail reconstruction, and Hierarchical Spatial Attention (HSA) for coordinate-aware spatial feature recalibration. An Adaptive Similarity Contrastive Loss (ASCL) is introduced to improve foreground--background feature discriminability under severe class imbalance. Experimental results on the AI CUP 2025 and VinDr-CXR benchmarks confirm the effectiveness of MASR-DNet. Furthermore, the model achieves competitive performance while maintaining a highly efficient parameter count compared to existing methods. These results confirm its potential as a robust and efficient solution for automated aortic valve and cardiomegaly detection in clinical imaging.Our code is available at: https://github.com/thinhdoanvu/MASR-DNet

title: AI Dominion vs. Human Dominion: Charting the Future of Artificial Intelligence: A Crossroad of Progress and Concerns
affiliations: State University of New York at Buffalo School of Law

detail.title: AI Dominion vs. Human Dominion: Charting the Future of Artificial Intelligence: A Crossroad of Progress and Concerns
detail.abstract: How far do international systems and social structures change by incorporating Artificial Intelligence in an era of rapid technological progress? Exponential and unprecedented AI uptake, predominantly of generative models, creates enormous innovation but exposes intricate issues related to economic inequality and eroding trust. This paper examines this interaction comprehensively, highlighting the sharp chasm between rapid technological development and underlying regulatory frameworks, thus underscoring the importance of anticipatory governance. Does artificial intelligence bring a new economic paradigm with the potential to reduce wage inequality and increase wealth concentration? Artificial intelligence has the potential to lower wage differentials by taking over better-paid employment; however, it could, at the same time, increase the concentration of wealth through unequal returns on investment. Algorithmic pricing creates a new and often hidden kind of implicit collusion, making it harder to interpret and apply antitrust laws. How do current legal frameworks resolve artificial intelligence's "creative double bind" on intellectual property, the obscurity of liability, and the fragmentation of global governance? AI's broad data absorption and potentially market-substituting outputs challenge copyright law and threaten to erode creators' incentives. Assigning liability for ambiguous autonomous systems is difficult, suggesting the necessity of novel accountability structures beyond traditional product liability. The emerging "patchwork" of disparate state-level rules, particularly in the United States, adds to compliance and uniform protection complexity. What significant challenges does artificial intelligence pose to democratic discourse and the maintenance of social trust through the refinement of bias and distortion of information? AI systems, made with historically skewed sets of information, risk amplifying systemic inequality and creating further problems, including "digital redlining." What strategies can counter the rapid spread of misinformation and deepfakes created through generative AI? How can we protect the integrity of our information ecosystem while technological developments continue to advance? In what ways does disinformation strengthen social polarizations, and what might we do to mitigate these divisions? What role should states, technology firms, and individuals play in ensuring the responsible development of artificial intelligence? How might we methodically analyze and address the built-in dangers of generative AI? What frameworks should be developed to foster human-focused development in the AI sector? What strategies should be considered to address these daunting challenges? This paper calls for a four-part reform strategy: (i) simplifying the morass surrounding intellectual property and liability law; (ii) reviewing antitrust legislation about the potential risks of algorithmic collusion; (iii) harmonizing fragmented regimes; (iv) strengthening human oversight, requiring proactive steps to minimize bias while investing in umbrella AI literacy initiatives. A new framework called the "Autonomy Passport," along with ongoing surveillance and emergency recall procedures, emerges as a viable national response to the responsible and secure deployment of AI technologies. Moreover, a prospective examination of the labor market is necessary to assuage fears of job replacement. This research thoroughly addresses the complex challenges and calls for developing resilient, human-centered governance regimes. If we tap into the transformative potential of artificial intelligence, we can drive inclusive economic growth and improve social welfare. It emphasizes the urgent need for practical international cooperation and provides a platform for forthcoming multi-disciplinary investigation, thus strengthening our ability to explore new spheres of positive social impact.

title: Anomalies and the Decision to Go Public
affiliations: North Carolina State University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Augusta University - James M. Hull College of Business

detail.title: Anomalies and the Decision to Go Public
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether stock market mispricing affects private firms’ decisions to go public. We construct a peer-based mispricing measure from a broad set of return anomalies and show that private firms are more likely to initiate an IPO when public peers are more overvalued. The predictability weakens after the academic publication of the underlying anomaly signals, consistent with information dissemination increasing arbitrage activity and reducing mispricing-induced issuance. We further find that peer-based anomaly signals predict long-run post-IPO returns but do not predict post-IPO investment, supporting a strategic market-timing interpretation rather than a financing-needs story. Overall, our results suggest that inefficiencies in the secondary market can distort capital allocation in the primary market.

title: A Panel Covariance Adjustment for Weak-Instrument-Robust Inference in Proxy SVARs

detail.title: A Panel Covariance Adjustment for Weak-Instrument-Robust Inference in Proxy SVARs
detail.abstract: Proxy SVARs identified with external instruments are widely used to estimate the dynamic effects of macroeconomic shocks, but valid inference remains difficult when the instrument is weak. Montiel Olea et al. (2021) develop weak-instrument-robust confidence sets for impulse-responses in time-series proxy SVARs. This paper extends their framework to panel proxy SVARs in which the external instrument and the target shock variable are common across cross-sectional units. In this setting, the relevant identifying variation remains time-series variation even though estimation is conducted on a stacked panel. Hence, applying the time-series covariance construction directly to stacked panel observations can overstate the effective instrument strength and understate impulse-response uncertainty. I propose a panel covariance adjustment that aggregates the relevant score contributions within each time period and estimates their long-run variance over time. The resulting procedure preserves the Montiel Olea et al. (2021) Anderson-Rubin confidence-set inversion while adapting the covariance estimator to the dependence structure induced by a common target shock and instrument pair in panel data. I establish asymptotic validity under fixed-N-large-T asymptotics and potentially weak proxies. An empirical illustration using quarterly U.S. macroeconomic national- and state-level data on oil-supply-news shocks shows that the adjustment substantially changes first-stage relevance diagnostics and yields panel impulse-response confidence sets that reveal dynamics less visible in aggregate time-series data.

title: The Care Work Employment Trap: How Childcare Hours Determine Female Labour Market Participation in India

detail.title: The Care Work Employment Trap: How Childcare Hours Determine Female Labour Market Participation in India
detail.abstract: Care work is the binding structural constraint on female employment in India, yet its causal magnitude has been obscured by a focus on cultural and marital explanations. Using India's 2024 Time Use Survey (10.2 million activity observations), we estimate that each additional hour of childcare and eldercare reduces female employment probability by 5.5 percentage points-a penalty confirmed across multiple specifications with state fixed effects (n = 103,731). The equivalent male coefficient is-0.08 pp and statistically indistinguishable from zero, establishing a clean gender asymmetry. Marriage does not amplify this penalty (care × married interaction near-zero, p = 0.52), but education deepens it: the care × higher-education interaction is-6.8 pp (p < 0.001), consistent with educated women substituting cognitive supervisory care which is harder to delegate-for physical care. Monotonicity analysis confirms that women in the highest care burden quartile face a 22.9 percent employment rate versus 28.4 percent for those with zero care minutes. State-level heterogeneity is large, with the marginal penalty ranging from-19 pp to near-zero, identifying states were care infrastructure has succeeded in decoupling care work from employment exclusion. These findings reframe the female employment problem in India: the constraint is not marriage or culture per se, but the unequal allocation of undelegable care hours.

title: SAARC vs BIMSTEC: Why Regional Integration is Failing in South Asia

detail.title: SAARC vs BIMSTEC: Why Regional Integration is Failing in South Asia
detail.abstract: This article examines the persistent failure of regional integration in South Asia through a comparative analysis of South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation and Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation. Despite strong growth potential, intra-regional trade remains low due to structural, political, and institutional barriers. SAARC’s stagnation is largely driven by geopolitical tensions, particularly between India and Pakistan, along with its consensus-based decision-making system. BIMSTEC, designed to bypass these challenges and enhance connectivity, has also failed to achieve meaningful integration due to slow institutional progress, protectionist policies, and instability in Myanmar. High tariffs, poor infrastructure, and limited trade complementarity further weaken both frameworks. The article argues that without shifting from rhetorical commitments to pragmatic cooperation—especially in trade facilitation, connectivity, and energy—regional initiatives will remain ineffective, leaving South Asia’s significant economic potential unrealized.

title: Dispersion of News Sentiment and Stock Price Return: Applying a Deep Learning Approach
affiliations: Texas A&M University, USA and Cleveland State University

detail.title: Dispersion of News Sentiment and Stock Price Return: Applying a Deep Learning Approach
detail.abstract: We examine whether the temporal structure of firm-level news sentiment contains predictive information for stock returns around earnings announcements. Rather than summarizing sentiment using static dispersion measures, we model the full sequence of pre-announcement sentiment using a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network. Using sentiment scores derived from Wall Street Journal articles, we construct daily firm-level sentiment sequences and form portfolios based on model-implied return signals. The sequence-based strategy generates economically large and statistically significant long-short return spreads out of sample, outperforming a benchmark based on sentiment dispersion. The results suggest that the dynamics of information arrival, rather than static disagreement proxies, play a central role in post-announcement price adjustment.

title: Does Prosperity Buy Gender Equality? Class Gradients in India's Unpaid Care Burden

detail.title: Does Prosperity Buy Gender Equality? Class Gradients in India's Unpaid Care Burden
detail.abstract: Higher socioeconomic status buys Indian women freedom from scrubbing-but not from supervising. Using a 5% random sample of India's 2024 Time Use Survey, we document a systematic divergence in the class gradient of unpaid work across activity types. For domestic (household maintenance) work, the gender gap narrows modestly at higher SES, consistent with egalitarian substitution: affluent couples outsource physical tasks and both partners reduce absolute time. For childcare, however, the class gradient is flat or slightly adverse for women: higher-SES mothers maintain or intensify supervisory and developmental childcare even as their physical domestic burden falls-consistent with Lareau's (2003) intensive cultivation model. A placebo regression using personal care and sleep time (Activity 1-digit code 9)-a gender-neutral activity-yields a near-zero Female × High-SES interaction, validating the methodology. Robustness checks (urban-only, rural-only, married-only, North vs. South India, 10% replication sample, continuous SES) confirm the domestic/childcare divergence. The policy implication is direct: income growth and education alone will not close India's childcare gender gap-public care infrastructure is the missing lever.

title: Networks of Stock Prices in the Capital Market

detail.title: Networks of Stock Prices in the Capital Market
detail.abstract: The collective movement of stock prices harbors complex interdependencies that are conventionally simplified only through a linear lens. This paper explores structural network representations in the Indonesian capital market by testing the limits of Pearson correlation and Mutual Information (MI) in unveiling the spectral dynamics of the market. Across 2,328 rolling observation windows from 2015 to 2025, we examine 24 methodological configurations that combine three dependency estimators (Pearson, MI adaptive binning, and MI-kNN), two graph filtering schemes (Minimum Spanning Tree/MST and Planar Maximally Filtered Graph/PMFG), and four community decoders. The empirical results unveil a fundamental reality: topological richness does not always resonate with sectoral classification precision. The Pearson, MST, and Infomap configuration is shown to remain the most robust foundation for recovering conventional sectoral taxonomy. Nevertheless, when deeper observation demands the exposition of local structures and the weave of heterogeneous communities, the architectural relaxation through PMFG demonstrates its superiority. In the realm of residual information detection, MI adaptive binning appears far more proportional than kNN; histogram-based regularization successfully tames empirical noise without sweeping away traces of non-linear dependency. Ultimately, the synergy of MI and PMFG is not positioned to dethrone the dominance of linear correlation, but rather to provide an essential analytical lens for excavating hidden economic sub-structures-such as the cohesion of commodity regimes-that have long transcended the rigid boundaries of the market's formal sectors.

title: The Grandparent Care Economy: Conditional Effects on Women's Childcare Burden in India

detail.title: The Grandparent Care Economy: Conditional Effects on Women's Childcare Burden in India
detail.abstract: Using India's 2024 Time Use Survey (full nationally representative dataset, n = 123,463 women aged 18-50 in child-present households), we investigate whether coresident grandparents reduce the childcare burden on mothers. A pooled regression yields a modest negative average effect (-3.5 min/day, n.s.), but this masks a meaningful conditional relationship. Decomposing by maternal employment status, we find that grandparent co-residence reduces daily childcare minutes for non-employed mothers by approximately 7 minutes (p < 0.001), while employed mothers show essentially zero net effect (+0.1 min, n.s.). The conditional grandparent effect for non-employed mothers is statistically significant and robust to state fixed effects and demographic controls. Rural households drive the significant grandparent effect (-7.0 minutes/day, p < 0.001); urban estimates are near-zero (-0.2 min, n.s.), consistent with different multi-generational household dynamics across sectors. These findings reframe the "grandparent care economy": grandparents primarily function as a direct care substitute for non-employed mothers, not as a labor market enabler for already-working mothers. The employment split explains why a pooled coefficient understates the conditional relationship: employed women have already compressed childcare time through work absence, leaving little room for grandparent-enabled substitution. Policy implications differ accordingly.

title: The Invisible Mental Load: Gender Gaps in Multitasking and Simultaneous Activity Patterns in India

detail.title: The Invisible Mental Load: Gender Gaps in Multitasking and Simultaneous Activity Patterns in India
detail.abstract: Using India's 2024 Time Use Survey, we document an unexpected pattern in multitasking behavior: men engage in simultaneous activities more frequently than women, contrary to Western literature showing mothers multitask more than fathers. Men spend 12.1% of their time multitasking compared to women's 11.2%, with 46.7% of men's episodes involving simultaneous activities versus 40.1% for women. Robustness checks reveal this male "multitasking premium" is driven by combining leisure activities (watching TV while socializing), while women perform care work sequentially because tasks require focused attention. These finding challenges simplistic interpretations of multitasking as time poverty: men's optional leisure fragmentation differs fundamentally from women's constrained sequential care work. Within women, employed and educated women multitask more than non-employed women, supporting double burden theory. We argue standard simultaneous activity flags miss women's fragmented time: rapid task-switching between cooking, childcare, and household management appears "sequential" in 30-minute blocks but reflects severe time poverty. The invisible "mental load” planning, coordinating, remembering creates cognitive burden not captured by simultaneous activity measures. Our findings suggest measuring time fragmentation requires methods beyond simple simultaneity flags, and that gender gaps in time poverty persist even when traditional multitasking measures show men’s higher rates.

detail.abstract: The current stage of development of the tax system of Ukraine is characterized by large-scale processes of digital transformation, which have become an integral component of fiscal modernization and integration into the European economic space. The digitalization of tax administration is seen as a key factor in increasing the transparency, efficiency and fairness of taxation, as well as a tool for ensuring fiscal stability in the face of global challenges. In the context of the implementation of the EU-Ukraine Association Agreement and the provisions of the Directive on Administrative Cooperation in the field of Taxation (DAC6-DAC8), the Common Reporting Standard (CRS), and the Standard Audit File for Tax (SAF-T), the digital reform of the tax sector is becoming systemic, covering both technological and institutional and legal aspects. Based on the official statistics of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, the European Commission, the World Bank, the IMF, and the Ministry of Finance of Ukraine, the author assesses the level of digital maturity of the fiscal system. The integral index of digital integration of tax services is calculated, which for Ukraine is 0.63, which is lower than the average level in the European Union of 0.82, but indicates a gradual convergence of administration standards and improvement of the quality of electronic services. A comparative analysis of the implementation of European standards has shown that Ukraine has made significant progress in creating basic electronic tools, but needs to deepen data integration, introduce artificial intelligence for risk analysis, and strengthen cybersecurity of tax information. It is substantiated that successful digitalization of the tax system requires a holistic data policy, a combination of technological, organizational and regulatory changes. The transition to an intelligent tax ecosystem will increase the efficiency of administration, reduce the level of the shadow economy and strengthen the fiscal security of Ukraine.

title: The Sleep Penalty: How Marriage and Care Work Deprive Indian Women of Rest

detail.title: The Sleep Penalty: How Marriage and Care Work Deprive Indian Women of Rest
detail.abstract: Using a 5% sample of India's 2024 Time Use Survey, we document a sleep penalty of approximately 21 minutes per night for married women relative to married men (Female × Married interaction, full model with state fixed effects, p < 0.001). This is substantially larger than the-3.2 minutes originally reported in an underspecified model. The penalty is concentrated in rural areas (-24 min, significant) and among non-employed married women (-60 min), suggesting night-time care obligations rather than total care work hours are the primary driver. The penalty peaks at ages 30-39 (-42 min, p=0.008), corresponding to peak childcare intensity. Contrary to the original claim, care work hours measured in daytime time diaries do not fully mediate the penalty-the Female × Married coefficient remains significant after care controls-pointing to sleep fragmentation from night-time duties as a distinct channel. Policies targeting maternal sleep deprivation should prioritize rural women, mothers of young children, and postnatal support services.
